category: Enterprise Architecture, System Hardening & Advanced Threats

content.tldr: A rootkit is stealth malware engineered to conceal processes, files, and unauthorized access by intercepting operating system API calls or executing in kernel/hypervisor ring 0.
content.simple_explanation: Unlike standard malware that runs in user space (Ring 3), advanced rootkits hook kernel data structures (Ring 0) or hypervisors (Ring -1). By intercepting system call tables (e.g. sys_call_table in Linux or SSDT in Windows), the rootkit alters the responses returned to administrative tools. When an administrator runs `ps` or `netstat`, the rootkit intercepts the call and deletes its own process IDs, open ports, and file descriptors from the output.
content.real_world_example: A burglar who taps the bank's CCTV surveillance feed: when the security guard looks at the monitor, the hacked feed loops tranquil footage of an empty vault while the burglar works undetected.
content.why_it_matters_and_pitfalls: Detecting a kernel rootkit from within the infected operating system is inherently unreliable because the kernel itself lies to security tools. Detection requires out-of-band analysis: live memory dump acquisition (Volatility), hardware TPM Measured Boot, or running antivirus from an external trusted boot environment.
